claim: 38.9% of studies used nonvalidated assessment instruments or composite scores from different instruments to assess ACEs.
source: In 50% of the studies only very few or even single ACE types were assessed (e.g. institutional rearing or low SES) - 38.9% using nonvalidated assessment instruments or composite scores from different instruments.
evidence: This is a summary of data from the quality assessment.

claim: Across a number of threat-related learning paradigms (n=21 studies), a consistent finding emerged of reduced discrimination between signals of threat and safety (i.e. CS+ and CS-) in individuals reporting ACEs.
source: Across a number of threat-related learning paradigms (n=21 studies), a consistent finding emerged of reduced discrimination between signals of threat and safety (i.e. CS+ and CS-) in individuals reporting ACEs.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple studies in the review.

claim: Reduced discrimination was rather consistently driven by blunted responding to cues signaling threat (i.e. CS+, anticipation of a negative image) in psychophysiological fear responses as measured with SCR.
source: Reduced discrimination was rather consistently driven by blunted responding to cues signaling threat (i.e. CS+, anticipation of a negative image) in psychophysiological fear responses as measured with SCR (Harnett et al., 2019; Klingelhöfer-Jens et al., 2023; Kuehl et al., 2020; Machlin et al., 2019; McLaughlin et al., 2016), FPS (Lis et al., 2020; Stout et al., 2021; Thome et al., 2018), as well as self-reported fear ratings (Qiu et al., 2023; see Figure 2E for outcome measures used across studies).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: Blunted responding to threat cues was observed in samples of adults reporting ACEs as children (6 out of 10 studies) as well as children and adolescents (3 out of 5 studies).
source: These results originate from samples of adults reporting ACEs as children (6 out of 10 studies) as well as children and adolescents (3 out of 5 studies; see Supplementary file 3 and Supplementary file 4 for details).
evidence: This is a summary of data from the review.

claim: Three studies reported enhanced rather than reduced discrimination between signals of threat and safety in exposed individuals reporting a history of ACEs.
source: However, three additional studies reported enhanced rather than reduced discrimination between signals of threat and safety in exposed individuals reporting a history of ACEs in SCRs (Marusak et al., 2021) and FPS (Zoladz et al., 2022) in females, but not males (Morrison et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: Severity of ACEs was negatively correlated with responsiveness to danger signals.
source: Furthermore, although only rarely analyzed, severity of ACEs was also negatively correlated with responsiveness to danger signals (McLaughlin et al., 2016; Qiu et al., 2023; but see Estrada et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: A substantial number of studies report no effects of ACEs on fear acquisition for at least one out of several outcome measures.
source: A substantial number of studies also report no effects of ACEs on fear acquisition for at least one out of several outcome measures, including SCR (Bremner et al., 2005; Estrada et al., 2020; Huskey et al., 2022; Morrison et al., 2022; Scharfenort et al., 2016b), FPS (Deslauriers et al., 2018; Huskey et al., 2022; Jovanovic et al., 2009; Kuehl et al., 2020; Morrison et al., 2022; Rowland et al., 2022; Stenson et al., 2021; Thome et al., 2018; Zoladz et al., 2022), heart rate (Huskey et al., 2022), ratings of valence and arousal (Klingelhöfer-Jens et al., 2023; Qiu et al., 2023; Schellhaas et al., 2022), fear (McLaughlin et al., 2016; Scharfenort et al., 2016b), expectancy/contingency (Huskey et al., 2022; Klingelhöfer-Jens et al., 2023; Zoladz et al., 2022) as well as null findings also during re-acquisition (Bremner et al., 2005) and behavioral distance (Marusak et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a summary of null findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: Two studies suggest developmental effects of ACEs on threat learning in which successful CS discrimination at an earlier than typical age (i.e. already at 4–5 years) was observed.
source: In addition, two studies suggest developmental effects of ACEs on threat learning in which successful CS discrimination at an earlier than typical age (i.e. already at 4–5 years, Machlin et al., 2019) and more adult-like functional connectivity between the hippocampus and prefrontal regions (Silvers et al., 2016) was observed.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: Two studies suggest developmental effects of ACEs on threat learning in which more adult-like functional connectivity between the hippocampus and prefrontal regions was observed.
source: In addition, two studies suggest developmental effects of ACEs on threat learning in which successful CS discrimination at an earlier than typical age (i.e. already at 4–5 years, Machlin et al., 2019) and more adult-like functional connectivity between the hippocampus and prefrontal regions (Silvers et al., 2016) was observed.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: Patterns of reduced discrimination between signals of threat and safety following threat learning in individuals reporting ACEs also emerges in generalization phases (5 out of 7 studies).
source: Patterns of reduced discrimination between signals of threat and safety following threat learning in individuals reporting ACEs also emerges in generalization phases (5 out of 7 studies: Klingelhöfer-Jens et al., 2023; Lange et al., 2019; Qiu et al., 2023; Thome et al., 2018; Zoladz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: Reduced discrimination in generalization phases was mostly driven by blunted CS+ responding in SCRs, lower US expectancy ratings, blunted valence and arousal ratings to the CS+ as well as enhanced ratings to the CS-.
source: This was, however, again mostly driven by blunted CS+ responding in SCRs (Klingelhöfer-Jens et al., 2023), lower US expectancy ratings (Qiu et al., 2023), blunted valence and arousal ratings to the CS+ as well as enhanced ratings to the CS- (Lange et al., 2019) rather than differences in generalization gradients.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: Generally no differences in generalization gradients were observed in these studies.
source: Interestingly, generally no differences in generalization gradients were observed in these studies, even though one study (Zoladz et al., 2022) claims enhanced generalization in exposed females.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the review.

claim: On a behavioral level, trauma-exposed individuals reported highest threat uncertainty (longer reaction times) to highly-ambiguous GSs, while healthy controls reported most uncertainty when rating GSs that were most similar to the CS+.
source: On a behavioral level, trauma-exposed individuals reported highest threat uncertainty (longer reaction times) to highly-ambiguous GSs, while healthy controls reported most uncertainty when rating GSs that were most similar to the CS+ (Thome et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: Individuals reporting a history of ACEs show reduced discrimination between learned signals of danger and safety, primarily driven by blunted responding to signals of danger during fear acquisition training and generalization.
source: In sum, a converging pattern emerged across studies whereby individuals reporting a history of ACEs show reduced discrimination between learned signals of danger and safety, primarily driven by blunted responding to signals of danger during fear acquisition training and generalization.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the review findings.

claim: Most studies report no effects of ACEs on extinction learning.
source: For the extinction phase (N=12, whereof six do not report acquisition results), most studies report no effects of ACEs on extinction learning (SCR: Bremner et al., 2005; Huskey et al., 2022; Kuehl et al., 2020; Marusak et al., 2021; McLaughlin et al., 2016; Scharfenort et al., 2016b; Susman et al., 2021; FPS: France et al., 2022; Huskey et al., 2022; Kuehl et al., 2020; ratings of fear: Scharfenort et al., 2016b; McLaughlin et al., 2016 expectancy: Huskey et al., 2022; as well as heart rate: Bremner et al., 2005; Huskey et al., 2022; or behavioral distance: Marusak et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: One study reports higher US expectancy to the CS- with an increasing number of experienced traumatic events and enhanced behavioral distance to the CS+ as compared to the CS- during extinction recall for children reporting a history of ACEs.
source: Of the three studies that observed a significant association between ACEs and fear extinction, one reports higher US expectancy to the CS- with an increasing number of experienced traumatic events. The same study demonstrated an enhanced behavioral distance to the CS+ as compared to the CS- during extinction recall (but not extinction) for children reporting a history of ACEs compared to children reporting no history of ACEs (Marusak et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: Two studies report enhanced SCR to the CS+ in children with a history of ACEs during extinction.
source: Two other studies report enhanced SCR to the CS+ in children with a history of ACEs during extinction (Jenness et al., 2019; Milojevich et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: A number of studies report heightened general (physiological) reactivity in ACE exposed individuals.
source: In addition to the overall pattern of blunted threat-learning, a number of studies also report heightened general (physiological) reactivity in ACE exposed individuals (FPS: Jovanovic et al., 2009; Kreutzer and Gorka, 2021; Pole et al., 2007; Rowland et al., 2022; Wolitzky-Taylor et al., 2014, interaction effects: Young et al., 2019; Zoladz et al., 2022, descriptive evidence: Morrison et al., 2022; SCR:Estrada et al., 2020, i.e. decreased habituation, interaction effects:Jovanovic et al., 2020; Scharfenort et al., 2016b; Young et al., 2019 and risk ratings:Lis et al., 2020; Thome et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: Kreutzer and Gorka, 2021 observed generally enhanced startle reactivity in individuals that have experienced interpersonal trauma (and higher trauma load), but blunted responding in individuals exposed to other trauma types (and lower trauma load) as compared to controls.
source: Of note, Kreutzer and Gorka, 2021 observed generally enhanced startle reactivity in individuals that have experienced interpersonal trauma (and higher trauma load), but blunted responding in individuals exposed to other trauma types (and lower trauma load) as compared to controls.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: Jovanovic et al., 2022 report a negative correlation of startle reactivity towards the CS+ and trauma exposure, but only in participants aware of experimental contingencies, while they report the opposite pattern for unaware participants.
source: In addition, Jovanovic et al., 2022 report a negative correlation of startle reactivity towards the CS+ and trauma exposure, but only in participants aware of experimental contingencies, while they report the opposite pattern for unaware participants.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: Decreased general reactivity is only reported by one study using SCR.
source: Decreased general reactivity, however, is only reported by one study using SCR (Klingelhöfer-Jens et al., 2023) and some studies report null findings (all outcome measures: Young et al., 2018; Huskey et al., 2022; Jovanovic et al., 2022; FPS and contingency ratings: Jovanovic et al., 2009; valence, arousal, contingency ratings: Klingelhöfer-Jens et al., 2023, heart rate: Young et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: Results for both amygdala and hippocampus activation during acquisition training were inconsistent across studies.
source: Results (see Figure 2E) for both amygdala and hippocampus activation during acquisition training were inconsistent across studies.
evidence: This is a summary of neuroimaging findings from the review.

claim: For the amygdala, blunted CS discrimination and learning slopes as well as enhanced or reduced reactivity in individuals reporting ACEs and null findings are reported.
source: For the amygdala, blunted CS discrimination and learning slopes (DeCross et al., 2022) as well as enhanced (Bremner et al., 2005) or reduced reactivity in individuals reporting ACEs (Harnett et al., 2019) and null findings (Silvers et al., 2016) are reported.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: For the hippocampus, higher activation for CS+ vs. CS- in individuals reporting ACEs or a negative association with ACEs and null findings are reported.
source: For the hippocampus, higher activation for CS+ vs. CS- in individuals reporting ACEs (Silvers et al., 2016) or a negative association with ACEs (Harnett et al., 2019) and null findings (DeCross et al., 2022; Scharfenort et al., 2016b) are reported.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: Negative associations of neural activation with ACEs are reported for the dorsolateral and ventromedial prefrontal cortex.
source: Negative associations of neural activation with ACEs are further reported for the dorsolateral and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (Harnett et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: During fear generalization, no associations between ACEs were observed with (re-)activation of the amygdala, vmPFC, insula, dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC), hippocampus, or vmPFC.
source: During fear generalization, no associations between ACEs were observed with (re-)activation of the amygdala, vmPFC (Lange et al., 2019), insula, dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC), hippocampus, or vmPFC (Morey et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: During extinction recall, children reporting ACEs showed stronger (re-)activation in the dACC and the insula (but not in other regions of interest (ROIs)) to the extinguished CS+ as compared to controls in absence of group differences for the CS-.
source: During extinction recall, children reporting ACEs showed stronger (re-)activation in the dACC and the insula (but not in other regions of interest (ROIs)) to the extinguished CS+ as compared to controls in absence of group differences for the CS- (Marusak et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: For fear acquisition, nine studies reported blunted responses to the threat cue in individuals with a history of ACEs (in any outcome measure).
source: For fear acquisition, a total of 21 studies reported results. Of these studies, nine studies reported blunted responses to the threat cue in individuals with a history of ACEs (in any outcome measure).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the review.

claim: For fear acquisition, three studies report enhanced responding to the threat cue in individuals with a history of ACEs.
source: In contrast, three studies report enhanced responding to the threat cue in individuals with a history of ACEs (even though methodological challenges hamper a clearcut interpretation of these results, see introduction and discussion for details).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the review.

claim: For threat generalization, five out of seven studies reported blunted responding to threat cues in individuals reporting ACEs compared to controls.
source: For threat generalization, a total of seven studies reported results for a generalization phase. Of those, five reported blunted responding to threat cues in individuals reporting ACEs compared to controls.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the review.

claim: The results point towards generally blunted threat learning.
source: In sum, we conclude that the results point towards generally blunted threat learning (see also likelihood ratio tests in Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the review findings, supported by likelihood ratio tests.

claim: Fourteen out of 28 studies reporting behavioral results show blunted responding to rewarding feedback following adverse experiences during childhood.
source: Fourteen out of 28 studies reporting behavioral results show blunted responding to rewarding feedback following adverse experiences during childhood (see Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the review.

claim: The most commonly employed indicators of reward learning performance are measures of task performance (i.e. number of correct responses, points or reward earned) and speed of learning i.e, reaction time or learning rate.
source: The most commonly employed indicators of reward learning performance in these studies are measures of task performance (i.e. number of correct responses, points or reward earned) and speed of learning i.e, reaction time or learning rate (Delgado et al., 2022; Dennison et al., 2019; Harms et al., 2018; Patterson et al., 2013; Pechtel and Pizzagalli, 2013; Sheridan et al., 2018; Weiss et al., 2019; White et al., 2022; Wilkinson et al., 2021; Wismer Fries and Pollak, 2017).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: Deficient reward expectation or the violation thereof (i.e., prediction error) in the ACE group was restricted to studies employing reinforcement learning models.
source: Deficient reward expectation or the violation thereof (i.e., prediction error) in the ACE group was restricted to studies employing reinforcement learning models (Hanson et al., 2017; Letkiewicz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: In an exploration-exploitation task, reduced exploration and learning rate in exposed individuals is interpreted as a less optimal strategy to maximize rewards.
source: Furthermore, in an exploration-exploitation task, reduced exploration and learning rate in exposed individuals is interpreted as a less optimal strategy to maximize rewards (Lloyd et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: In an incentive saccade task, exposed individuals show reduced responsiveness to rewarding feedback and less improvement of error performance under positive reinforcement.
source: In addition, in an incentive saccade task, exposed individuals show reduced responsiveness to rewarding feedback and less improvement of error performance under positive reinforcement (Mueller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: One study reports that exposed participants rated rewarding cues as less positive in a MID task.
source: One study (Dillon et al., 2009) reports that exposed participants rated rewarding cues as less positive in a MID task.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: The same number of studies (n=14) report null results for the association between ACEs and reward learning performance.
source: Importantly, the same number of studies (n=14) report null results for the association between ACEs and reward learning performance.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the review.

claim: Outcome measures were comparable between studies reporting significant and null findings.
source: Outcome measures were comparable between studies reporting significant and null findings e.g., response times, success rate or number of errors (Bjork et al., 2008; Boecker-Schlier et al., 2016; Cisler et al., 2019; Dennison et al., 2016; Dillon et al., 2009; Gonzalez et al., 2016; Mehta et al., 2010; Morris et al., 2015; Müller et al., 2015; Smith and Pollak, 2022; Weiland et al., 2013), measures of reward expectation and prediction error (Cisler et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the review.

claim: While active reward learning seems to be affected by ACEs, reinforcement learning in the context of passive avoidance may not be.
source: A more unique set of outcome measures – commission and omission errors - obtained from passive avoidance tasks was used in two studies with null findings (Blair et al., 2022; Gerin et al., 2017), which might suggest that while active reward learning seems to be affected by ACEs, reinforcement learning in the context of passive avoidance may not be.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the pattern of findings.

claim: Ten studies provide evidence for reduced neural (re)activation during the anticipation of a rewarding outcome following ACEs in distributed areas as well as in dedicated reward-processing circuitry including the ventral striatum and the insula.
source: Ten of these studies provide evidence for reduced neural (re)activation during the anticipation of a rewarding outcome following ACEs in distributed areas (Birn et al., 2017; Casement et al., 2014; Dillon et al., 2009; Mehta et al., 2010; Morelli et al., 2021) as well as in dedicated reward-processing circuitry including the ventral striatum and the insula (Boecker-Schlier et al., 2016; Gerin et al., 2017; Martz et al., 2022; Mullins et al., 2020; Yau et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: Six studies show enhanced (re)activation (e.g. in the thalamus, midbrain, insula, ventral striatum, inferior and medial frontal gyrus, dorsolateral prefrontal gyrus) during reward anticipation.
source: In contrast, six studies show enhanced (re)activation (e.g. in the thalamus, midbrain, insula, ventral striatum, inferior and medial frontal gyrus, dorsolateral prefrontal gyrus) during reward anticipation (Casement et al., 2014; DelDonno et al., 2019; Gonzalez et al., 2016; Hendrikse et al., 2022; Kwarteng et al., 2021; Romens et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: Three studies show ACE-related enhanced brain (re)activation (i.e. inferior frontal, cingulate and superior temporal gyrus as well as, prefrontal cortex, thalamus, putamen) during loss feedback or prediction errors.
source: Three studies show ACE-related enhanced brain (re)activation (i.e. inferior frontal, cingulate and superior temporal gyrus as well as, prefrontal cortex, thalamus, putamen) during loss feedback or prediction errors (Birn et al., 2017; Gerin et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2021) including a linear relationship between number of traumatic events and ventral ACC activation (Eckstrand et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: Four studies show no difference between exposed participants and an unexposed control group during reward anticipation and delivery.
source: An additional four studies show no difference between exposed participants and an unexposed control group during reward anticipation (Bjork et al., 2008; Müller et al., 2015; Weiland et al., 2013) and delivery (Boecker-Schlier et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: The current systematic literature review suggests evidence for reduced learning associated with rewards in participants with a history of ACEs.
source: Together, the current systematic literature review suggests evidence for reduced learning associated with rewards in participants with a history of ACEs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the review findings.

claim: This finding is consistent with a recent meta-analysis that included 14 of the 43 studies reviewed here but had a broader focus on reward processing in general.
source: This finding is consistent with a recent meta-analysis (Oltean et al., 2023) that included 14 of the 43 studies reviewed here but had a broader focus on reward processing in general.
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from a cited meta-analysis.

claim: A total of 28 studies obtained and reported behavioral measures of reward learning performance, of which 14 studies reported a significant reduction in reward learning or the valuation of rewarding outcomes.
source: A total of 28 studies obtained and reported behavioral measures of reward learning performance. Of those studies, 14 studies reported a significant reduction in reward learning or the valuation of rewarding outcomes.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the review.

claim: Fourteen studies reported no significant group differences or associations with ACEs in reward learning.
source: Fourteen studies reported no significant group differences or associations with ACEs in reward learning.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the review.

claim: Blunted reward learning in individuals reporting ACEs emerges as a consistent pattern of results.
source: Therefore, we conclude that blunted reward learning in individuals reporting ACEs emerges as a consistent pattern of results.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the review findings.

claim: 10 out of 17 studies suggest reduced (re-)activation in (not only) reward-related brain regions during the anticipation of a rewarding outcome.
source: A more inconsistent pattern of results could be detected for fMRI activation patterns: 10 out of 17 studies suggest reduced (re-)activation in (not only) reward-related brain regions during the anticipation of a rewarding outcome.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the review.

claim: Seven studies showed enhanced activation in midbrain regions and the activation of a wider brain network during reward anticipation.
source: At the same time, seven studies showed the opposite result pattern with enhanced activation in midbrain regions and the activation of a wider brain network during reward anticipation.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the review.

claim: The results point towards generally blunted reward learning.
source: In sum, we conclude that the results point towards generally blunted reward learning (see also likelihood ratio tests in Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the review findings, supported by likelihood ratio tests.

claim: Reporting a history of ACEs appears to be associated with enduring effects on the capacity to differentiate environmental cues for aversive and safe outcomes.
source: Thus, reporting a history of ACEs appears to be associated with enduring effects on the capacity to differentiate environmental cues for aversive and safe outcomes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the review findings.

claim: The pattern of blunted conditioned threat responding in individuals with ACEs is distinct from what is typically observed in patients suffering from anxiety and stress-related disorders.
source: Of note, this pattern is distinct from what is typically observed in patients suffering from anxiety and stress-related disorders - enhanced responding specifically to the learned safety signal (e.g., Duits et al., 2015), which likewise results in reduced CS discrimination.
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from cited literature on anxiety disorders.

claim: Threat learning processes in individuals with a history of ACEs are distinct from those generally observed in anxiety patients.
source: Hence, we suggest that threat learning processes in individuals with a history of ACEs are distinct from those generally observed in anxiety patients.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the review findings.

claim: Exposed individuals may represent a distinct sub-group of patients which has so far been understudied due to a strong focus on group level inferences and a lack of studies aiming to identify and utilize individual-level heterogeneity in response pattern.
source: As ACEs are considered a potent risk factor for the development of psychopathology (e.g., Teicher et al., 2022), we speculate that exposed individuals may represent a distinct sub-group of patients which has so far been understudied due to a strong focus on group level inferences (patients vs. controls) and a lack of studies aiming to identify and utilize individual-level heterogeneity in response pattern.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the implications of the findings.

claim: Reduced reward learning performance presented itself as reduced accuracy or reward earned and speed of learning in individuals with a history of ACEs.
source: Reduced reward learning performance presented itself as reduced accuracy or reward earned and speed of learning in individuals with a history of ACEs which can be interpreted as blunted responding to, and integration of, reinforcing reward information.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the review.

claim: Reduced reward learning performance can be interpreted as blunted responding to, and integration of, reinforcing reward information.
source: Reduced reward learning performance presented itself as reduced accuracy or reward earned and speed of learning in individuals with a history of ACEs which can be interpreted as blunted responding to, and integration of, reinforcing reward information.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Evidence from several studies indicates that individuals with a history of ACEs show hyperresponsivity to losses, suggesting that the differences in reward anticipation are not due to diminished hedonic value but rather reflect reduction in incentive salience.
source: Further, evidence from several studies indicates that individuals with a history of ACEs show hyperresponsivity to losses, suggesting that the differences in reward anticipation are not due to diminished hedonic value (Birn et al., 2017) but rather reflect reduction in incentive salience (Olney et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of findings from cited studies.

claim: Individuals that report ACEs rate rewarding cues - not the reward itself - as less positive than unexposed individuals.
source: This interpretation is further supported by a study showing that individuals that report ACEs rate rewarding cues - not the reward itself - as less positive than unexposed individuals (Dillon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: ACEs might have affected the development of the dopaminergic system.
source: A more far-reaching interpretation would be that ACEs might have affected the development of the dopaminergic system, which has been discussed as a consequence of childhood adversity more broadly (for a discussion see Smith and Pollak, 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation, with citation to relevant discussion.

claim: From a neuropathological perspective, the collected findings are in line with findings in anhedonia which is similarly characterized by selective impairments in reinforced actions rather than reward responsiveness.
source: From a neuropathological perspective, the collected findings are in line with findings in anhedonia which is similarly characterized by selective impairments in reinforced actions rather than reward responsiveness (Pizzagalli, 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from cited literature on anhedonia.

claim: The pattern of blunted behavioral responding to threat or rewards emerges independent of diverse sample or paradigm choices.
source: Integrating the results from two research fields, we can conclude that the pattern of blunted behavioral responding to threat or rewards emerges independent of diverse sample or paradigm choices.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from integrating findings across the review.

claim: A rather converging pattern was observed not only in the threat learning field but also in the reward learning field despite diversity of the employed paradigms.
source: It is hence noteworthy that a rather converging pattern was observed not only in the threat learning field - in which similar paradigms are applied across studies - but also in the reward learning field despite diversity of the employed paradigms and hence the specific sub-processes investigated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the review findings.

claim: ACEs seem to be linked to generally blunted learning from threat and reward.
source: We thus conclude that ACEs seem to be linked to generally blunted learning from threat and reward.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the review findings.

claim: The often unpredictable nature of environments featuring adverse conditions may render it more adaptive to dampen behavioral modification by the erratic and infrequent signals of threat and reward.
source: The often unpredictable nature of environments featuring adverse conditions may render it more adaptive to dampen behavioral modification by the erratic and infrequent signals of threat and reward.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the adaptive nature of the observed pattern.

claim: The pattern of blunted threat and reward learning in individuals reporting a history of ACEs may represent a coping strategy to environmental demands.
source: It can hence be speculated that the pattern of blunted threat and reward learning in individuals reporting a history of ACEs may represent a coping strategy to environmental demands.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Blunted threat and reward learning constitutes a potentially modifiable experience-dependent plasticity process that is at the core of many well established clinical interventions such as cognitive behavioral therapy.
source: From a therapeutic perspective, blunted threat and reward learning constitutes a potentially modifiable experience-dependent plasticity process that is at the core of many well established clinical interventions such as cognitive behavioral therapy and hence holds promise to be targeted in clinical interventions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about clinical implications.

claim: Discrimination training may enhance the ability to discriminate between signals of threat and safety which may prevent overgeneralization.
source: More specifically, discrimination training may enhance the ability to discriminate between signals of threat and safety which may prevent overgeneralization.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential interventions.

claim: The systematic literature review does not find evidence for distinct effects of specific ACEs with either reward or threat learning performance.
source: Importantly, our systematic literature review does not find evidence for distinct effects of specific ACEs with either reward or threat learning performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the review findings.

claim: Four out of nine studies focusing exclusively on threat-related ACEs show blunted responding to threat-cues in individuals with a history of ACEs.
source: In the threat learning field, four out of nine studies focusing exclusively on threat-related ACEs show blunted responding to threat-cues in individuals with a history of ACEs (Kuehl et al., 2020; Lis et al., 2020; McLaughlin, 2016; Thome et al., 2018), while three studies report null-findings (Jovanovic et al., 2009; Rowland et al., 2022; Stenson et al., 2021) and two studies enhanced threat responding (Marusak et al., 2021; Morrison et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: One study investigating the relationship between deprivation-related ACEs and threat learning reports reduced CS discrimination driven by blunted responding to cues signaling threat in self-reported fear ratings in individuals with a history of ACEs as compared to controls.
source: The pattern of results from the two available studies focusing exclusively on deprivation-related ACEs is comparable: One study investigating the relationship between deprivation-related ACEs and threat learning reports reduced CS discrimination driven by blunted responding to cues signaling threat in self-reported fear ratings in individuals with a history of ACEs as compared to controls (Qiu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: Four studies investigating associations between deprivation-specific experience and behavioral indices of reward learning show reduced behavioral reward learning performance in the group exposed to deprivation experiences.
source: The pattern of results in the seven studies investigating associations between deprivation-specific experience and behavioral indices of reward learning also seem to match the general pattern of results reported here. Four studies (Delgado et al., 2022; Sheridan et al., 2018; White et al., 2022; Wismer Fries and Pollak, 2017) show reduced behavioral reward learning performance in the group exposed to deprivation experiences while three studies show no differences at the behavioral level (Gonzalez et al., 2016; Mehta et al., 2010; Smith and Pollak, 2022).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: Of the studies focusing on threat-only experiences, four studies showed blunted responding, while only one study revealed a null result.
source: Of the studies focusing on threat-only experiences, four studies (Hanson et al., 2017; Harms et al., 2018; Letkiewicz et al., 2022; Pechtel and Pizzagalli, 2013) showed blunted responding, while only one study (Cisler et al., 2019) revealed a null result.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: The results from the systematic literature search point towards generally blunted threat- and reward learning in individuals reporting a history of ACEs irrespective of the specific type of ACE (i.e. threat vs. deprivation).
source: Hence, we conclude that the results from the systematic literature search point towards generally blunted threat- and reward learning in individuals reporting a history of ACEs and blunted reward and threat learning - irrespective of the specific type of ACE (i.e. threat vs. deprivation; see also likelihood ratio tests in Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the review findings, supported by likelihood ratio tests.

claim: Most studies included in this review did not differentiate explicitly between adversity subtypes which does not allow us to draw firm conclusions on this from the literature.
source: Yet, most studies included in this review did not differentiate explicitly between adversity subtypes which does not allow us to draw firm conclusions on this from the literature.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on the review findings.

claim: The observed pattern of results stands in contrast to predictions by prominent theoretical accounts in the field (DMAP) that posit distinct (neuro-) biological effects of different ACE types.
source: This observed pattern of results, however, stands in contrast to predictions by prominent theoretical accounts in the field (DMAP, Sheridan and McLaughlin, 2014; McLaughlin et al., 2014) that posit distinct (neuro-) biological effects of different ACE types.
evidence: This is a comparison of the review findings with theoretical predictions from cited literature.

claim: One challenge that has been highlighted is that certain aspects of ACEs are inseparable and can be conceptualized as different sides of the same coin.
source: In brief, one challenge that has been highlighted is that certain aspects of ACEs are inseparable and can be conceptualized as different sides of the same coin.
evidence: This is a discussion of challenges in the field, drawing on broader literature.

claim: There is little evidence for the core DMAP dimensions (i.e., deprivation and threat) mapping indeed onto specific neurobiological systems.
source: Additional criticism includes that there is little evidence for the core DMAP dimensions (i.e., deprivation and threat) mapping indeed onto specific neurobiological systems (Carozza et al., 2022; Smith and Pollak, 2021) or clinical outcomes (Witt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a criticism of DMAP supported by citations.

claim: There is little evidence for the core DMAP dimensions mapping onto specific clinical outcomes.
source: Additional criticism includes that there is little evidence for the core DMAP dimensions (i.e., deprivation and threat) mapping indeed onto specific neurobiological systems (Carozza et al., 2022; Smith and Pollak, 2021) or clinical outcomes (Witt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a criticism of DMAP supported by citations.

claim: A wealth of research suggests that the effects of experiences of early life adversity are cumulative, non-specific and rather unlikely to be tied to specific types of adverse events.
source: In addition a wealth of research suggests that the effects of experiences of early life adversity are cumulative, non-specific and rather unlikely to be tied to specific types of adverse events (Danese et al., 2009; Danese and Widom, 2020; Gehred et al., 2021; Smith and Pollak, 2022; Young et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant research.

claim: The ratios of studies reporting blunted threat responding during fear acquisition vs null findings were similar across pediatric (3 out of 5) and adult samples (6 out of 10).
source: In the current literature search, studies from the threat field relied approximately equally often on pediatric samples (i.e. children or adolescents), and adults with a history of ACEs (see Figure 1A and B) and the ratios of studies reporting blunted threat responding during fear acquisition vs null findings were similar across pediatric (3 out of 5) and adult samples (6 out of 10).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the review.

claim: The ratios of children/adolescent to adult samples did not differ between studies who report blunted behavioral responding (12:5) vs null results (11:5) in the reward field.
source: However, the ratios of children/adolescent to adult samples did not differ between studies who report blunted behavioral responding (12:5) vs null results (11:5) in the reward field.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the review.

claim: The literature review provides no evidence that the reported associations between ACEs and either threat or reward learning processes, or their direction may vary as a function of developmental timing of ACEs or recency of the experiences.
source: Thus, our literature review provides no evidence that the reported associations between ACEs and either threat or reward learning processes, or their direction may vary as a function of developmental timing of ACEs or recency of the experiences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the review findings.

claim: A recently published meta-analysis reported adversity-related alterations in amygdala and PFC BOLD activation in emotion processing, memory processing, inhibitory control, and reward processing tasks only in adult samples, but not in children or adolescents.
source: However, these behavioral findings stand in contrast to a recently published meta-analysis reporting adversity-related alterations in amygdala and PFC BOLD activation in emotion processing, memory processing, inhibitory control, and reward processing tasks only in adult samples (having experienced adversity recently or during childhood), but not in children or adolescents (Gee, 2021; Hosseini-Kamkar et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited meta-analysis.

claim: There is evidence in the literature that an effect of developmental timing of ACEs might exist at the neural level.
source: At the same time, there is evidence in the literature that such an effect might exist at the neural level (Hosseini-Kamkar et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a statement about evidence from cited literature.

claim: The pattern of results observed does not seem to differ depending on the outcome measure.
source: Even though it is well known that different outcome measures tap into different underlying processes (Lonsdorf et al., 2017), the pattern of results observed does not seem to differ depending on the outcome measure.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the review findings.

claim: Different outcome measures might be differentially sensitive to individual differences vs. group effects.
source: It should be noted though that these different outcome measures might be differentially sensitive to individual differences vs. group effects.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about methodological considerations.

claim: There is no universally objectively most reliable measure for threat learning outcomes.
source: Recently, the reliability of different outcome measures (i.e. SCR, fear ratings and BOLD fMRI) was compared (Klingelhöfer-Jens et al., 2022; see also Flournoy et al., 2024 for BOLD fMRI only) with the conclusion that there is no universally objectively most reliable measure, even though some specifications led to more reliable estimates.
evidence: This is a finding from cited studies on measurement reliability.

claim: The systematic inventory of ACE operationalization highlights substantial heterogeneity in assessment tools and operationalization as a general challenge for cross-study comparison and drawing broad inference across this field.
source: Our systematic inventory of ACE operationalization in the field of threat and reward learning (see Figures 3 and 4 as well as Supplementary file 2 for a list of questionnaires used in the included studies) highlights substantial heterogeneity in assessment tools and operationalization as a general challenge for cross-study comparison and drawing broad inference across this field (Koppold et al., 2023; Smith and Pollak, 2022).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the systematic inventory, supported by citations.

claim: The operationalization of ACEs varied greatly between studies (e.g. dimensional vs. categorical and specific vs. general adversity types).
source: Likewise, the operationalization of ACEs varied greatly between studies (e.g. dimensional vs. categorical and specific vs. general adversity types) and often involved the generation of (artificial) groups from a continuous variable (Cohen, 1983) by median-split dichotomization (Jovanovic et al., 2020; Lange et al., 2019) or by applying cut-offs - that may vary even for a single questionnaire (e.g., CTQ, Bernstein et al., 1997; Bernstein and Fink, 1998).
evidence: This is a summary of methodological practices observed in the review, with citations.

claim: Data reduction approaches may obscure meaningful variability.
source: These data reduction approaches may obscure meaningful variability (Gee, 2021) and render the composition of adequate control groups challenging.
evidence: This is a methodological concern supported by citation.

claim: Studies focusing on deprivation-related ACEs oftentimes did not assess potential additional threat-related experiences.
source: More precisely, studies focusing on deprivation-related ACEs oftentimes did not assess potential additional threat-related experiences.
evidence: This is an observation about methodological practices in the reviewed studies.

claim: Studies focusing on threat-related ACEs typically did not assess potential additional deprivation-related experience.
source: Further the studies focusing on threat-related ACEs typically did not assess potential additional deprivation-related experience.
evidence: This is an observation about methodological practices in the reviewed studies.

claim: Control and ACE groups may be characterized by similar overall levels of ACEs and may only differ with regard to one specific ACE.
source: As a consequence, control and ACE groups may be characterized by similar overall levels of ACEs and may only differ with regard to one specific ACE (Kuehl et al., 2020; Marusak et al., 2021; McLaughlin et al., 2016; Morrison et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference about potential confounding in the reviewed studies, with citations.

claim: Participants assigned to the control group might have had severe adverse experiences not screened for.
source: In other words, participants assigned to the control group might have had severe adverse experiences not screened for (e.g. Jovanovic et al., 2020; Zoladz et al., 2022; Stout et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference about potential confounding in the reviewed studies, with citations.

claim: This lack of broad screening might be particularly problematic as there is little support for distinct neurobiological effects of different adversity types.
source: This lack of broad screening might be particularly problematic as there is little support for distinct neurobiological effects of different adversity types as discussed above.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of methodological practices, drawing on earlier discussion.
